text: The A Century of Progress International Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, was a world's fair held in Chicago, Illinois, United States, from 1933 to 1934, celebrating the city's centennial and registered under the Bureau International des Expositions (BIE). Designed primarily in Art Deco and Moderne styles, the fair promoted technological innovation as its theme, with the motto "Science Finds, Industry Applies, Man Conforms," emphasizing the connection between science and American life. Its architectural symbol was the Sky Ride, a transporter bridge perpendicular to Lake Michigan’s shore allowing passage between sides. The fair was organized as an Illinois nonprofit corporation in January 1928 and held on a 427-acre (1.73 km²) portion of Burnham Park, located on three and a half miles of newly reclaimed land between 12th and 39th streets on the Near South Side. Opened on May 27, 1933, by U.S. Postmaster General James Farley at a four-hour ceremony at Soldier Field, the fair’s opening night featured automatic lighting triggered by the star Arcturus, chosen because its light began its journey around the time of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. The rays were detected by photoelectric cells in astronomical observatories and converted into electrical energy transmitted to Chicago. The fair buildings were multi-colored, creating a "Rainbow City" contrast to the "White City" of the 1893 fair, and were constructed using five-ply Douglas fir plywood, ribbed-metal siding, and prefabricated materials like Masonite, Sheetrock, and Maizewood, with windowless but brightly lit structures. The architectural commission, led by Paul Cret and Raymond Hood, included Edward Bennett, John Holabird, and Hubert Burnham, and excluded Frank Lloyd Wright due to his poor collaboration skills, though he developed three conceptual designs. The commission emphasized modern, forward-looking architecture rather than past styles, enabled by the fair’s location on state-owned, code-free land. Key pavilions included the Hall of Science (Cret), Federal Building (Bennett, Burnham, Holabird), General Motors Building (Albert Kahn), Sears Pavilion (Nimmons, Carr, Wright), the twelve-sided House of Tomorrow (George Frederick Keck), Italian Pavilion (Mario de Renzi and Adalberto Libera), Belgian Village (Burnham Brothers with Alfons De Rijdt), and Streets of Paris (Andrew Rebori and John W. Root), where Sally Rand performed. The fair also featured exhibits such as the "Lincoln Group" reconstructing Lincoln’s birth cabin, the Lincoln-Berry General Store, the Chicago Wigwam, and the Rutledge Tavern, and a replica of Jean Baptiste Point du Sable’s cabin, following a campaign by African American groups. The fair included the arrival of the German airship Graf Zeppelin on October 26, 1933, which landed at Curtiss-Wright Airport in Glenview for twenty-five minutes before departing. American automobile manufacturers showcased "dream cars," including a Rollston-bodied Duesenberg called the Twenty Grand, Cadillac’s V-16 limousine, Nash’s vertical parking garage, Lincoln’s rear-engined concept car precursor to the Lincoln-Zephyr, and Pierce-Arrow’s "Suddenly it's 1940!" Silver Arrow, with Packard winning best of show for its Packard Twelve. The 1933 Homes of Tomorrow Exhibition displayed modern home designs and materials. Marine artist Hilda Goldblatt Gorenstein painted twelve murals for the Navy exhibit depicting sea power from Jamestown in 1607 through World War I, and William Mark Young painted murals for the Ohio State Exhibit, later relocated to the Ohio Statehouse. The first Major League Baseball All-Star Game was held at Comiskey Park. In May 1934, the Union Pacific Railroad exhibited its streamlined M-10000 and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad’s Zephyr, which completed a record-breaking 13-hour 5-minute run from Denver to Chicago on May 26, known as the "Dawn-to-Dusk Dash," arriving at the fair’s "Wings of a Century" pageant. Both trains entered revenue service as the City of Salina and the Pioneer Zephyr, the latter now on display at the Museum of Science and Industry. Frank Buck’s Jungle Camp, visited by over two million people, was later moved to Amityville, New York. From June to November 1933, an amoebic dysentery outbreak affected over a thousand people, resulting in 98 deaths, eventually controlled by Joel Connolly through the discovery of defective plumbing contaminating drinking water. Originally scheduled to close on November 12, 1933, the fair reopened from May 26 to October 31, 1934, due to its success. It was financed through membership sales, raising over $800,000 (equal to $18,803,980 today), and a $10 million bond issued on October 28, 1929, before the stock market crash, with half retired by 1933 and the full debt paid by 1934—making it the first international fair in U.S. history to pay for itself. The fair attracted 48,769,227 visitors, with 22,565,859 admissions during the 170 days from May 27, 1933, and 16,486,377 during the 163 days from May 26, 1934, totaling 39,052,236. Much of the site is now part of Northerly Island Park and McCormick Place; the Balbo Monument, given by Benito Mussolini to honor General Italo Balbo’s 1933 trans-Atlantic flight, remains near Soldier Field, and Chicago added a third red star to its flag in 1933, now represented by the fourth of four stars. The Italian-American community donated a statue of Christopher Columbus to Grant Park. The Polish Museum of America holds Stanisław Kaczor-Batowski’s painting of Pulaski at Savannah, which won first place at the fair and was later unveiled by Eleanor Roosevelt at the Art Institute of Chicago in July 1934, before being purchased by the Polish Women's Alliance. The U.S. Post Office issued a fifty-cent Air Mail stamp (Scott C-18), informally known as the Baby Zep, depicting the fair’s Federal Building, the Graf Zeppelin in flight, and its hangar in Friedrichshafen, Germany, along with 1-cent and 3-cent commemorative stamps showing Fort Dearborn and the Federal Building, printed in souvenir sheets of 25 (Scott 728–31), later reprinted in 1935 (Scott 766–67). From October 2010 to September 2011, the National Building Museum in Washington, D.C. hosted an exhibition titled Designing Tomorrow: America's World's Fairs of the 1930s, prominently featuring the Century of Progress fair. The official records and papers of Lenox Lohr, general manager of the fair, are archived in Special Collections at the University of Illinois, Chicago, and materials including photographs, guidebooks, maps, architectural drawings, and souvenirs are held by the Ryerson & Burnham Libraries at the Art Institute of Chicago, with specific collections including the Chicago Architects Oral History Project, Daniel H. Burnham Jr. and Hubert Burnham Papers, Edward H. Bennett Collection, and Voorhees, Gmelin, and Walker photographs.
